name: Jude
v: From Jude, a slave of Jesus the Messiah and brother of James — to those who are called, who are loved by God the Father and kept safe in Jesus the Messiah:
Mercy, peace, and love — may they flood over you.
My beloved, I was eager to write to you about the salvation we share, but I find I must instead write urging you to fight for the faith — the faith handed down once and for all to God's holy people.

Certain men have slipped in among you unnoticed — long ago marked out for this judgment. They are godless. They twist the grace of our God into a license for filth, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus the Messiah.
You already know all this, but let me remind you: the Lord rescued his people out of Egypt — and afterward destroyed the ones who refused to believe.
And the angels — the ones who would not stay in their assigned place but abandoned their proper home — he has locked them in everlasting chains, in darkness, awaiting the judgment of the great Day.

Same with Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns nearby. They gave themselves over to sexual corruption, chased after flesh that was not theirs — and now they lie there as the public exhibit of what eternal fire looks like.
Yet these dreamers do the very same thing. They defile their bodies. They despise authority. They sneer at glorious beings.
Even Michael the archangel — when he was disputing with the devil over Moses' body — did not dare to throw a slanderous verdict at him. All he said was, "The Lord rebuke you."
But these people slander whatever they do not understand. And whatever they do understand — by raw instinct, like animals — is exactly what destroys them.
Hell awaits them. They have walked the road of Cain. They have thrown themselves headlong into Balaam's error for profit. They have perished in Korah's rebellion.

They are the hidden reefs at your love feasts, eating shamelessly alongside you, feeding only themselves. Clouds without rain, blown along by the wind. Trees in late autumn — no fruit, twice dead, uprooted.
Wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own disgrace. Wandering stars, for whom the blackest darkness has been kept in reserve forever.
Enoch — the seventh from Adam — prophesied about these men too: "Look — the Lord comes with thousands upon thousands of his holy ones,
to bring judgment on everyone, to convict every soul of every godless deed they committed in their godlessness, and of every harsh word godless sinners have spoken against him."
These are the grumblers, the complainers, chasing their own appetites. Their mouths spew arrogance. They flatter people when there is something to be gained.
But you, my beloved — remember what the apostles of our Lord Jesus the Messiah said would happen.
They told you: "In the last days, mockers will come, chasing after their own godless cravings."
These are the ones who split the community, ruled by instinct, with no Spirit in them.
But you, my beloved — build yourselves up on your most holy faith. Pray in the Holy Spirit.
Keep yourselves anchored in the love of God as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus the Messiah, which leads to eternal life.
Have mercy on those who waver.
Snatch others out of the fire and save them. To still others, show mercy — but with fear, hating even the clothing stained by their flesh.
Now to the One who can keep you from falling and present you before his glorious presence — flawless and overflowing with joy —
to the only God our Savior, through Jesus the Messiah our Lord, be glory, majesty, power, and authority — before all time, now, and into every age to come. Amen.

com.d:
# Jude 1 – Called and Kept

The opening of Jude's letter carries a profound assertion about identity: we are called, loved, and kept by God in a way that defines our deepest reality. In just a few words, Jude establishes who his readers are, not by their accomplishments or feelings, but by their relationship to the Father and the security found in Christ's protection.

Notice the tender confidence woven through these opening words. To be "called" speaks of God's initiative—not something we earned but something He chose for us. To be "loved by God the Father" anchors us in the affection at the heart of the universe. And to be "kept safe for Jesus Christ" means we rest in an active, dynamic protection that extends from this moment through eternity. This is not a distant, impersonal arrangement but an intimate bond. The Father calls us, loves us personally, and keeps us secure.

This opening becomes even more significant when we realize Jude wrote to warn believers about spiritual danger—false teachers, moral compromise, and subtle deceptions threatening the church. Yet instead of beginning with alarm, he begins with assurance. Before naming the problems, he anchors his readers in their true identity. This is pastoral wisdom: we face spiritual danger most effectively when we know we are already called and kept.

In our own lives, when we face uncertainty, temptation, or confusion about whether God still holds us, Jude's opening word is medicine. The Christian life is not built on our ability to hold on to God; it is built on God's unshakeable grip on us. Our calling is not revoked by our stumbling. Our Father's love is not contingent on our performance. We are kept safe—not because we have it all figured out, but because Christ holds us.

What would change in how you face today if you truly believed you are called, loved, and kept? How might this truth reshape your confidence when you feel vulnerable or afraid?
com.s:
The Epistle of Jude opens with a carefully constructed salutation that establishes both the author's identity and his theological framework for addressing the recipients. The writer identifies himself as "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James," a designation that most scholars understand as referencing Judas, the brother of Jesus mentioned in Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55. Rather than claiming familial authority through his biological relationship to the Lord, Jude adopts the humble self-designation *doulos* (δοῦλος), meaning "slave" or "servant," a term laden with Old Testament resonances connecting him to faithful servants of Yahweh while simultaneously acknowledging Christ's lordship.

The recipients are described through three participles that form a theologically rich triad: they are "called" (*klētois*, κλητοῖς), "beloved" (*ēgapēmenois*, ἠγαπημένοις), and "kept" (*tetērēmenois*, τετηρημένοις). This threefold description encompasses the full scope of salvation—divine initiative in calling, the Father's sustaining love, and preservation for Jesus Christ. The perfect passive participle *tetērēmenois* is particularly significant, as it anticipates the letter's later emphasis on God's keeping power in verse 24, forming an inclusio that brackets the epistle's urgent warnings about apostasy with assurances of divine protection.

The greeting itself—"mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you"—departs from the standard Pauline formula of "grace and peace," substituting "mercy" (*eleos*, ἔλεος) and adding "love" (*agapē*, ἀγάπη). Some interpreters suggest this variation reflects Jude's pastoral sensitivity to a community facing the unsettling presence of false teachers, where divine mercy becomes especially pertinent. The optative "be multiplied" (*plēthyntheiē*) echoes similar expressions in 1 Peter 1:2 and 2 Peter 1:2, leading some scholars to posit literary dependence or shared epistolary traditions within early Jewish Christianity.

The verse's canonical placement among the Catholic Epistles positions it as addressing not a single congregation but a broader Christian audience facing threats to doctrinal integrity. Jude's self-identification through James rather than directly through Jesus suggests an early date when such indirect authentication carried weight within communities familiar with the Jerusalem church's leadership structure.
com.p:
Jude's brief but fiery epistle emerges from the apostolic era, likely composed between AD 65–80, during the decades following Christ's resurrection and ascension when the church was expanding rapidly across the Roman world. This places the letter squarely within the church age, that pivotal epoch between Pentecost and the Parousia when the kingdom of God advances through the Spirit-empowered witness of Christ's body. Within the grand arc of redemption, Jude writes to believers living after the cross has been accomplished, after the Spirit has been poured out, yet before the final consummation when Christ returns to judge the living and dead.

The servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James opens with apostolic authority, addressing those who are "called, sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ." This triad of divine action echoes the eternal covenant purposes stretching from before creation into endless ages. The called ones represent the fulfillment of God's ancient promise to Abraham that through his seed all nations would be blessed—now Jew and Gentile alike are summoned into the commonwealth of Israel's Messiah.

Jude's urgent warning against false teachers who have "crept in unnoticed" carries profound typological weight. He summons three Old Testament judgments as warnings: Israel's wilderness generation who perished in unbelief, the angels who abandoned their proper dwelling, and Sodom and Gomorrah's destruction by fire. These historical judgments function as types of the final eschatological judgment awaiting all who reject God's authority. The wilderness generation who saw Egypt's plagues yet hardened their hearts prefigures those who taste kingdom realities yet apostatize. The angels' rebellion shadows the cosmic dimension of evil that will face ultimate defeat. Sodom's fiery overthrow typologically anticipates the eternal fire reserved for the ungodly.

Yet woven through this warning epistle shines glorious promise. The prophecy of Enoch concerning the Lord's coming "with ten thousands of His saints to execute judgment" points forward to the second advent when Christ descends with His holy ones to vindicate righteousness and condemn wickedness forever. This remains unfulfilled, awaiting that great Day.

The doxology crowning this letter anchors the church's hope: Christ is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them faultless before His glory with exceeding joy. For the church living between the advents, Jude's message resounds with urgent relevance—contend earnestly for the faith once delivered, guard against deception, and rest secure in the One who preserves His own until that glorious appearing.
